title: Reading graphs & tables in texts
examples: How do I make sure my answer directly uses the numbers shown?
What if the graph shows a trend but doesn't give exact numbers?
Can I use the graph to argue something that isn't clearly shown?

explain.say: Today we learn to read graphs and tables in texts. We will learn to use the data to support what the writer says. Look closely at what the graph shows you.
First, you must understand what the axes or headings mean. For example, one axis might show time passing by years. The other axis shows the amount of something measured.
Next, you need to find the specific data point the question asks about. If it asks about the highest point, you must locate that peak on the graph. It is a specific piece of evidence.
Then, you must connect that data point to the claim. You say something like, 'The graph shows X, which supports the claim that Y.' Do not just state the data.
For a table, you look at the row and the column headings. You find the intersection of the row and column you need. This gives you one clear fact.
In real life, think about a weather forecast chart. If the claim is 'It will be warmer next week,' you look at the temperature line for next week. That specific data supports the claim.

faq.q: Do I have to use the exact numbers from the graph?
faq.a: It is best to use the specific numbers if they are clear. If the graph only shows a general trend, describing the trend is fine.

faq.q: What if the claim is about a period, not just one point?
faq.a: You must describe the change over that entire period. For example, you could say it increased steadily from point A to point B.
asks: How do I talk about a range?

faq.q: Can I use a table to prove a point that the graph doesn't show?
faq.a: No. You must only use the data provided in the table or graph. Do not bring in outside knowledge.
asks: Must the data match the claim?

faq.q: What is the difference between describing data and making a claim?
faq.a: Describing data just says what the graph shows. Making a claim is interpreting what that data means for a bigger idea.
asks: How do I move from fact to idea?

faq.q: If the graph is confusing, what should I do?
faq.a: First, read the title and all the labels very carefully. If it is still confusing, it is better to state that the data is unclear.
asks: What if the scale is weird?

facts: Graphs use axes to show relationships between two variables.
Tables organize data into clear rows and columns for easy reading.
Linking data means using evidence to support a statement.
Always check the units of measurement on the axes or headings.

quiz.say: A graph shows rainfall amounts over ten years. The claim is that rainfall was generally low at the start. Which statement best uses the data?

options.show: The rainfall increased significantly over the decade.
options.say: The rainfall increased significantly over the decade.

options.show: The rainfall was highest in the middle years.
options.say: The rainfall was highest in the middle years.

options.show: The rainfall was stable throughout the whole period.
options.say: The rainfall was stable throughout the whole period.

options.show: The data shows the rainfall was low in the first few years.
options.say: The data shows the rainfall was low in the first few years.

quiz.why: This answer directly points to the initial data points, supporting the claim.

wrong.0: This ignores the starting data and focuses only on the end trend.
wrong.1: This introduces a point not mentioned in the claim or the data provided.
wrong.2: This contradicts the visual evidence of change shown in the graph.

quiz.say: A table shows student performance in five subjects. The claim is that the student performed best in English. Which statement best uses the data?

options.show: The student is good at most subjects.
options.say: The student is good at most subjects.

options.show: The student performed best in Maths.
options.say: The student performed best in Maths.

options.show: The student scored around 80 in all subjects.
options.say: The student scored around 80 in all subjects.

options.show: The table shows the highest score was achieved in English.
options.say: The table shows the highest score was achieved in English.

quiz.why: This answer correctly identifies the highest value and links it to the specific subject mentioned in the claim.

wrong.0: This is too general and does not pinpoint the single best performance as required.
wrong.1: This incorrectly chooses a different subject without evidence from the claim.
wrong.2: This averages the data instead of identifying the single highest point.

quiz.say: A graph tracks the speed of a car over time. The claim suggests the car slowed down rapidly between the first and second minute. Which statement best uses the data?

options.show: The graph shows a steep downward slope between the first and second minute.
options.say: The graph shows a steep downward slope between the first and second minute.

options.show: The car maintained a constant speed for two minutes.
options.say: The car maintained a constant speed for two minutes.

options.show: The car sped up slowly over the entire time.
options.say: The car sped up slowly over the entire time.

options.show: The speed was highest at the end of the second minute.
options.say: The speed was highest at the end of the second minute.

quiz.why: A steep downward slope visually represents a rapid decrease in speed, matching the claim.

wrong.1: The graph clearly shows a change in speed, not a constant rate.
wrong.2: This describes the opposite trend shown by the line graph.
wrong.3: The data shows the speed was decreasing, not reaching its peak at that time.
